issues.description: The problem statement describes a fully implemented Meal class and refers to Meal throughout the specification (including UML), but the template repository does not provide an implementation: Meal.java is empty and instead an Order class with the same structure is present. This name/type mismatch (Meal vs Order) will confuse students about which class to use and prevents them from following the specification that refers to Meal.
issues.suggestedFix: Provide a proper Meal.java implementation in the template that matches the class described in the problem statement (name, constructor, getters). Remove or rename the Order class in the template (or clearly document its purpose) so students are not confused by two equivalent classes with different names. Ensure the template aligns with the UML and references to Meal in the problem description.

issues.description: The problem statement and solution refer to a Meal class as the core entity for orders, but the template repository provides an Order class (template_repository/src/.../Order.java) instead of Meal. This divergent identifier for the same conceptual entity (a meal with a name and ingredient list) forces students to map 'Meal' to 'Order' across artifacts, creating unnecessary cognitive load and potential confusion when implementing required methods and classes (e.g., constructor signatures, getters, and references in Main).
issues.suggestedFix: Make the template use the same identifier as the problem statement and solution: rename the Order class/file to Meal (template_repository/src/.../Order.java -> template_repository/src/.../Meal.java) and update all usages (e.g., Main and any references) so students see a consistent Meal entity across problem, template, and solution. Alternatively, keep an Order wrapper but also provide a Meal class with identical shape to avoid naming mismatch.
